content: Red 2G is a synthetic red azo dye. It is water-soluble and exhibits slight solubility in ethanol. Typically, it is available as the disodium salt of 8-acetamido-1-hydroxy-2-phenyazonaphthalene-3,6-disulphonate. In the European Union, Red 2G is used as a food dye and is assigned the E number E128. However, its use is restricted to specific food products, such as breakfast sausages containing a minimum of 6% cereal content and burger meat with at least 4% vegetable and/or cereal content. Concerns regarding its safety were raised by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) in an opinion issued on July 5, 2007. In response, the European Commission proposed a draft regulation to suspend the use of E128 as a food coloring. This proposal was unanimously approved by EU Member States during a meeting of the Standing Committee on the Food Chain and Animal Health (Section Toxicological Safety of the Food Chain) on July 20, 2007. Red 2G is banned in several countries, including Australia, Austria, Canada, Japan, Norway, Sweden, Malaysia, and the United States. Additionally, it was banned in Ireland, Israel, and Greece in July 2007. The dye is relatively resistant to the bleaching effects of sulfur dioxide (E220) and sodium metabisulfite (E223). However, in the intestines, Red 2G can be metabolized into aniline, a toxic compound. This raises concerns that Red 2G may interfere with blood hemoglobin and potentially contribute to cancer development. Beyond its use as a food dye, Red 2G is also employed as a dye in coatings, inks, paper, crepe paper, and fine tissue. For example, it is a component of Masson's trichrome staining technique. From a health perspective, Red 2G is one of the colorants that the Hyperactive Children’s Support Group recommends eliminating from children’s diets. The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) has recently determined that E128 is potentially carcinogenic due to its conversion into aniline within the body when consumed.
